name: Retail

summary: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation are the volume use cases.

analysis.body:
The Census BTOS series provides a measured adoption figure for retail trade, NAICS 44-45. In the latest reading, 15.5% of retail firms answered yes to using AI in the last two weeks, up from 15.2% in the prior period. The question was first asked in September 2023, so the series offers a short but consistent fortnightly benchmark rather than a one-off estimate.

What retailers deploy AI for is documented across the trade sources. Per IHL Group, the focus includes inventory visibility, demand forecasting, pricing, delivery-date estimates, and store digital twins. The National Retail Federation tracks store automation, inventory computer vision, and customer-experience software. Coresight Research positions its work around AI in merchandising and supply-chain logistics, and its forum explores opportunities and challenges for consumer-focused businesses.

IHL Group's research points to where money and effort concentrate, and where they should. Its 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, in cooperation with Chain Store Age, finds inventory data accuracy, not AI budget size, separates specialty retail winners from laggards. IHL Group also reports that most retail AI budgets fund the wrong layer first, stalling pilots before they reach the store floor. Inventory distortion is down to $1.7 trillion, but empty shelves still cost $690.9 billion. Named deployments include Retailgrid's AI-powered spreadsheet and Price Radar at Nature's Emporium, Hanshow and Lingzhi Digital Technology building a store digital twin with 17,000 IoT devices at Rainbow's Shenzhen supermarket, and AfterShip's AI-powered delivery estimates at Dr. Squatch.

ROI evidence in the excerpts is specific but narrow. Per IHL Group, Dr. Squatch achieved a 31.89% recommendation click-through rate, attributed $32,978 in Q1 revenue, cut WISMO inquiries 25%, and reached 94% delivery-date accuracy using AfterShip's estimated delivery dates and tracking-page intelligence. No comparable ROI figures are given for the inventory or store digital twin examples, so the clearest quantified return comes from post-purchase delivery visibility and personalized recommendations.

The sources do not surface a detailed regulatory posture. Coresight Research frames AI as presenting opportunities and challenges for consumer-focused businesses, and the National Retail Federation's Paris conversations emphasize practical AI, connected stores, and relationship-driven loyalty rather than compliance. A reader deciding whether to deploy should take from this that adoption is real but still modest at 15.5%, that inventory data accuracy matters more than budget size per IHL Group, and that the most concrete ROI example is in delivery and recommendation features, not broad automation.

https://nrf.com/.brief: The National Retail Federation describes itself as an advocate for the people, policies, and ideas that support a thriving retail sector, and it provides retail news, insights, and industry events. According to the organization, conversations held in Paris illustrated how retailers are putting what it calls "The Next Now" into practice. These efforts span practical artificial intelligence, connected stores, and loyalty programs built on relationships.

https://coresight.com/.brief: Coresight Research says it delivers data-driven insights centered on retail and technology. It also claims deep expertise in China that it describes as unique in the industry. Additionally, the firm reports leading an invite-only, collaborative forum exploring AI opportunities and challenges for consumer-focused businesses.

https://ihlservices.com/.brief: IHL Group conducts research on retail technology spending and strategy. According to their 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, inventory data accuracy rather than AI budget size determines which specialty retailers succeed, and most retail AI budgets fund the wrong infrastructure layer first. The organisation also reports that inventory distortion has declined to $1.7 trillion, though empty shelves still cost $690.9 billion annually. IHL's analysis finds that the presence of AI does not predict pricing-platform quality among vendors, and retailers should instead evaluate explainability, automation controls, and governance safeguards.
